title: How Public Evals Work, Where They Break, and What Should Change
author: Eugene Yan
organization: eugeneyan.com (author is Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic)
pub_date: 2026-11-22 (article:published_time 2026-11-22T00:00:00Z; RSS pubDate Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000; date-only, no real time)
what_changed: A 42-minute teardown of 12 public agent benchmarks (Terminal Bench, DeepSWE, FrontierSWE, Terminal Bench Science, GDPval, Harvey LAB, AutomationBench, Agents' Last Exam, Finance Agent, HealthBench Professional, BrowseComp, OSWorld 2.0) with concrete grader-failure counts and recommendations on how practitioners should read and build evals.
mechanism: Decomposes eval tasks into instruction / environment / grader / optional reference; catalogs design principles (deterministic checks over LLM judges, outcome-not-steps grading, all-pass vs partial credit, difficulty mining); quantifies grader false negatives (unstated requirements, hidden tests clashing with agent-written tests, wrong answer keys) and false positives (string-contains assertions, rubric items that only check presence); argues for pass^k reliability, human-attention cost instead of dollar cost per task, multi-turn evals, negative tests (do-nothing and adversarial agents), transcript audits, and evaluating models inside your own production harness.
evidence_quality: High for a secondary synthesis: cites specific audit numbers from benchmark papers, Epoch AI reviews, Preference Model rebuild, Artificial Analysis, and the author's own review of dozens of failed DeepSWE trajectories. Several figures are attributed to third-party audits not re-checked here (UNVERIFIED beyond the post).
independent_confirmation: Partial. Latent Space AINews (2026-11-21) separately reports METR's finding that swarms overfit to self-generated tests and that horizons are longer on easy-to-verify tasks, consistent with the verification-gap theme. Individual audit numbers (e.g., 41/65 TBench 4.0 tasks on unstated requirements, >60% hallucination in Harvey LAB passes) not independently confirmed here: UNVERIFIED.
relevance: Very high. Directly actionable for anyone choosing models off leaderboards or building internal evals: add pass^k, audit tasks where several frontier models fail the same check, add do-nothing/adversarial negative tests, audit passing transcripts, avoid string-contains assertions, measure review/redo time rather than token cost, and benchmark inside your own harness.
overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to Edition 3's 'production cost per user vs eval cost per task' and 'verifying agent done claims' themes (the post explicitly argues cost-per-task is misleading and that agents declare false success). Materially new: grader-error audit data across 12 benchmarks and concrete grader-hardening techniques. Frame as 'how to read/fix evals', not a repeat of cost or done-claim verification.
summary: Eugene Yan studied 12 public evals and found evidence in 8 of them that the grader failed work that should have passed. Task anatomy: instruction (single-shot, no clarifying questions), environment (container/VM/docs), grader (code assertions, LLM judge on binary rubric, or both), optional human reference. Benchmarks now ship like software: Agents' Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57; Harvey LAB's public set grew from ~1,250 to 2,010 tasks since May 2026; Terminal Bench drops saturated tasks per version, breaking cross-version comparison. Principles: deterministic checks over LLM judges (DeepSWE and AutomationBench use none); grade outcome not steps; all-pass scoring is common (Harvey: 'no partial credit for catching most of the issues') but brittle; difficulty mining (BrowseComp kept only questions strongest models failed; HealthBench Professional made hard tasks ~3.5x more common). Model failure modes: skipping verification / stopping early (OSWorld 2.0, Harvey LAB, AutomationBench agents summarized partial lists as done) and dropping stated requirements (most common GDPval failure). Grader false negatives: 41 of 65 Terminal Bench 4.0 tasks graded on unstated requirements (Preference Model rebuild; making them explicit lifted one model from 63% to 89%); Epoch AI found scoring defects in 30 of 66 TBench tasks, 11 failing correct solutions; 23 of 113 DeepSWE tasks marked correct solutions as failures, and Epoch found hidden test files clash with agent-written tests in 18 of 113 tasks (penalizing agents that verify their own work), with an audit finding correct solutions failed in at least 20% of DeepSWE v1.1 tasks; OSWorld 2.0 had checks failing correct work in 23 of 108 tasks; BrowseComp trainers disagreed with the reference answer on 50 of 367 (14%); Terminal Bench Science has 128 task-fix issues on 57 of 70 tasks (79 verifier/instruction bugs), e.g. a verifier rejecting correct predictions in a different row order, and one run got 99 of 100 stars right and scored zero. False positives: Artificial Analysis found material hallucinations in >60% of Harvey LAB results that passed every criterion; 55% of AutomationBench assertions only check string contains/excludes (an email swapping counts '3' and '4' would pass); 44 of 65 Terminal Bench v4 tasks could be passed by cheating. Recommendations: report pass^k (two agents at 70% average: one reliable on 70% of tasks stays 70% at k=5, the other drops to 17%); cost per task misleads because models fail cheaply (17% of Agents' Last Exam failures were premature abandonment; on FrontierSWE one model submitted and stopped within 8 of 20 hours in 169 of 170 trials; on AutomationBench models declared success on 72-91% of analyzed failures; GDPval showed GPT-4o at ~1/10 GPT-5's cost per task but slower than an expert alone once review/redo time was included); verifiable tasks test implementation more than judgment (FrontierSWE's self-check tool spoon-feeds what to measure); real work is multi-turn (Laban et al.: 39% lower scores in simulated multi-turn); invest in graders: audit tasks where multiple frontier models fail the same check, add negative tests (do-nothing agent, adversarial agent), audit passing transcripts for reward hacking (FrontierSWE judge panel). Scores reflect model+harness: on Terminal Bench 2.0 one model scored 57.8% on neutral Terminus 2 vs 52.1% on its provider's harness, another 32.6% vs 19.6%; takeaway: evaluate models inside your own production harness. Also: FrontierSWE v2 switched from wall-clock to weighted instruction count for deterministic perf grading; author suggests scoring 1 - 1/speedup instead of capping at a target, and publishing partial credit alongside all-pass. GDPval human graders agreed 71% of the time; grader model agreed with them 66%.
